stories.title: Police exhume body of former Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk
stories.summary: The top diplomat was found dead on March 10, 1948, in the courtyard beneath his bathroom window, supposedly after a fall. Police said their probe aims to settle questions that have surrounded the death ever since.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KPEk Some historians believe Jan Masaryk, seen as a pro-Western figure, may have been killed by Soviet agents Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Czech police said Wednesday they had begun exhuming the remains of former Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk in an attempt to clear up speculation surrounding his death nearly 80 years ago. In a statement posted to X, police said they planned to examine the remains, buried at Prague 's Olsany Cemetery, "using the most modern forensic methods." "We believe that today's actions will bring us closer to clarifying the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Masaryk," the statement said. What happened to the former top diplomat? Masaryk was found dead on March 10, 1948, dressed only in his pajamas, in the courtyard at the Foreign Ministry beneath his bathroom window. The mysterious circumstances surrounding his death, at the height of the Cold War , have fueled speculation for decades. At the time, the Interior Ministry claimed that he had committed suicide. Others believed his fall may have been an accident, or that he was murdered by Soviet agents

But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade. Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. stories.article_text_excerpt: Nearly 5% of goods entering the EU are fake, costing businesses an estimated €83 billion annually. At the port of Alicante, OLAF and Spanish Customs officers sift through shipping containers, hunting for counterfeit products hidden in plain sight among legitimate trade. Experts describe illicit trade as a sophisticated global business model, no longer limited to luxury items but now spanning car parts, electronics, pharmaceuticals and food. Counterfeit car components pose particular risks, as they bypass safety testing entirely. Officials stress that buying fakes helps finance serious crimes, including drug and human trafficking, urging shoppers to think twice before chasing a bargain.
